intro: This last unit brings the whole course together. First you will meet Bill Cooper, a Navy and Air Force veteran whose shortwave broadcasts and 1991 book reached listeners and readers across the country. Many people still respect him. He warned his listeners about real government secrets, and he also passed on claims that have no evidence and one famous forgery. His life is a hard, honest test of everything you have learned about sorting claims.

You will read his story from service records, court papers and the work of historians. Then you will build a ledger with three columns: documented, disputed or unproven, and shown false. You will not be told what to think about him. You will be shown the evidence on each side, and you will do the sorting.

Then you will do your own capstone. You will choose one claim about a secret society from this course, trace it to its earliest source, gather evidence from more than one side and sort it into three piles. You will write and present an argument from evidence. Finally, you will practice disagreeing with respect. By the end you will be able to ask, about any claim you meet, how do we know?
bigQuestion: How can we tell a documented secret from an unproven or false claim, and how should we talk with people who see it differently?

timeline.t: Milton William Cooper is born in Long Beach, California.
The CIA approves MKUltra, a secret drug-testing program.
The Joint Chiefs propose Operation Northwoods; the Kennedy administration rejects it.
Cooper leaves the Air Force with an honorable discharge.
Cooper leaves the Navy with an honorable discharge.
The Senate's Church Committee reports on COINTELPRO and other intelligence abuses.
Anglia Television airs Alternative 3, a spoof documentary about a Mars colony.
Cooper posts his MJ-12 story online; the FBI and Air Force investigate the MJ-12 papers.
Behold a Pale Horse is published in Arizona.
The Northwoods memo is released to the public.
Cooper is charged with tax evasion and bank fraud and refuses to surrender.
Cooper dies on the night of 5 November in a shootout with deputies in Eagar, Arizona.

words.d: the official file the military keeps on a member, with dates, rank, units and awards
a statement that someone says is true
a second, independent source that backs up the first
false information spread on purpose to mislead
a formal charge by a grand jury saying there is enough evidence for a trial
a chart that sorts claims into columns by the evidence behind them
a document falsely made to look like the real work of someone else
the known history of where a document came from and who has held it
the first known appearance of a claim or story
able to be supported or undercut by evidence
the strongest opposing view, stated fairly
treating someone as foolish or beneath you

test.q: What do public records confirm about Bill Cooper's military career?
choices: He served honorably in the Air Force and the Navy
test.why: Records confirm his Air Force and Navy service and honorable discharges; the intelligence job is disputed.

test.q: Why is Cooper's naval intelligence story called unproven?
choices: No released record confirms it, and nothing proves it false
He never told it in public
test.why: No document places him on the team, but no evidence proves he never saw such papers.

test.q: What did Air Force investigators tell the FBI about MJ-12 in 1988?
choices: No such committee had ever been authorized or formed
test.why: The FBI's Majestic 12 file records this finding.

test.q: Which item from Cooper's book is a proven antisemitic forgery?
choices: The Protocols of the Elders of Zion
test.why: The Protocols were shown in 1921 to copy an 1864 French satire; a Bern court also ruled them a forgery in 1935.
Anglia Television aired it in 1977 as a scripted spoof with credited actors.

test.q: Which of Cooper's topics is documented by official records?
choices: Kennedy's driver firing the fatal shot
test.why: COINTELPRO is confirmed by FBI files and the Church Committee.

test.q: Why does the Northwoods memo not show Cooper had evidence for it in 1991?
choices: It was released in 1997, after his book
test.why: The memo became public six years after the book was published.

test.q: What is the difference between an indictment and a verdict?
choices: A verdict comes before a trial
An indictment is a charge; a verdict is a court's final decision on guilt
An indictment is a prison sentence
test.why: Cooper was indicted in 1998 but never tried, so there was no verdict.

test.q: Which claim is testable as written?
choices: Someone is always hiding the truth
The eye on the dollar was put there by the Illuminati
test.why: It names one object, one group and one action, so records can answer it.

test.q: What does a source chain help you find?
choices: The earliest source and any gaps where a guess became a fact
The most popular version of a claim
The shortest version of a claim
test.why: A source chain lists who repeated a claim, when and where they got it.

test.q: Where was the Eye of Providence first proposed for the Great Seal?
choices: In an Illuminati meeting in Bavaria
In a Masonic lodge in Boston
test.why: The first seal committee's report of 20 August 1776 proposes the eye.

test.q: How should a researcher report sources that disagree on a number?
choices: Pick the number that fits the argument
Report a range and name the sources
test.why: Honest handling of numbers builds credibility.

test.q: In the three-pile method, what does disputed mean?
choices: Serious people read the evidence differently
test.why: Disputed sits between documented and unsupported.

test.q: What did George Washington's 1798 letters to Snyder show?
choices: He believed the lodges spread Illuminati ideas
He accepted that the ideas had spread but doubted the lodges were spreading them
test.why: Washington separated a general worry from a specific charge he had no evidence for.

choices: You are right that some secrets were real; here is what the records show on this claim
I refuse to talk about it
test.why: It agrees where the evidence agrees, criticizes the claim rather than the person, and shares a source.

write.prompt: Choose one claim from this unit, either one of Bill Cooper's or the claim you tested in your capstone. Is it documented, disputed or unsupported? Cite at least two facts or sources from the unit, state the strongest counterclaim fairly, and explain your conclusion.
tips: Name each source with its author or body and its year.
Give the best evidence on both sides before you decide.
Use the unit's terms: documented, disputed, provenance, corroboration.
Let the evidence set the size of your claim; say what it cannot prove.
Criticize claims, never the people who believe them.

title: Bill Cooper and the Conspiracy Age, and Capstone

chapters.title: Bill Cooper: A Life and a Ledger
chapters.bigQuestion: When one writer mixes real government secrets with unproven and false claims, how can a reader sort one from the other?

story.title: A Voice on the Night Road
story.kicker: Somewhere on an interstate in the 1990s, a trucker turns a dial and finds a voice that tells him not to trust what he is told.
paragraphs: Picture a long-haul trucker crossing the plains after midnight in the mid-1990s. The FM stations have faded to hiss. He reaches for a shortwave radio wedged beside the seat. Shortwave signals bounce off the upper air at night, so a station hundreds of miles away can come in clear.

He turns the dial slowly past sermons, music and static. Then a calm, gravelly voice fills the cab. The speaker is a Navy veteran named Bill Cooper. He is talking about secret government programs, powerful private clubs and a hidden plan to rule the world. He tells his listeners to check everything for themselves.

Some of what the trucker hears that night is true. The CIA really did test drugs on people who did not know it. The FBI really did spy on American citizens. Other things he hears have no record behind them at all. And one book the voice recommends contains a famous forgery aimed at Jewish people.

The trucker cannot stop the rig to look anything up. He has only the voice and his own judgment. In this chapter you will have more tools than he did: service records, court papers, Senate reports and the work of historians. You will follow Cooper's life, then sort his claims into three piles, one claim at a time.
story.think: Why might a voice on late-night radio feel more trustworthy than a newspaper to some listeners? What would you want to check first?

lessons.title: A Military Childhood and the Air Force
lessons.mainIdea: Milton William Cooper was born in 1943, grew up in a military family and served in the Air Force until an honorable discharge in 1965.
reading: Milton William Cooper was born on 6 May 1943 in Long Beach, California. Friends and listeners later knew him as Bill. He grew up in a military family and moved often, as many service families do. That background shaped how he spoke. He talked like a veteran briefing other veterans, and many of his listeners had served too.

As a young man Cooper joined the U.S. Air Force. He served in the *Strategic Air Command*, the branch that ran long-range bombers and nuclear missiles during the Cold War. He later said he worked around B-52 bombers, tanker planes and Minuteman missiles and held a secret security clearance. He received an *honorable discharge* from the Air Force in 1965. An honorable discharge means a person left the service in good standing.

Historians separate two kinds of evidence about a life. A *service record* is the official file the military keeps on each member: dates, rank, units and awards. A personal account is what the person later says about that service. Both matter. The record shows what the military wrote down at the time. The account shows how the person understood and explained it. In Cooper's case the two line up well for the Air Force years. As the next lesson shows, they line up less well for his Navy years.

words.d: the Cold War branch of the U.S. Air Force that ran long-range bombers and nuclear missiles
leaving military service in good standing
the official file the military keeps on a member, with dates, rank, units and awards

look.title: Key Years in Cooper's Life
look.cite: Mark Jacobson, Pale Horse Rider (Blue Rider Press, 2018); Southern Poverty Law Center, Intelligence Report (2002)
look.prompt: How many years passed between Cooper leaving the Navy and publishing his book? What might a person's views go through in that much time?

check.q: Where and when was Bill Cooper born?
check.why: The reading says he was born on 6 May 1943 in Long Beach, California. Eagar is where he died.

check.q: What does an honorable discharge mean?
choices: The person was charged with a crime
The person left the service in good standing
The person was sent to a war zone
check.why: An honorable discharge means a person left military service in good standing.

check.q: What is the difference between a service record and a personal account?
choices: A service record is the military's official file; a personal account is what the person later says
A service record is a radio show; a personal account is a book
They are two names for the same document
A personal account is always more accurate than a service record
check.why: The reading defines the service record as the official file and the personal account as the person's own later telling.

lessons.title: What the Navy Records Show
lessons.mainIdea: Public Navy records show Cooper served honorably, including a tour in Vietnam, but they do not show the intelligence job he later described.
reading: After the Air Force, Cooper joined the U.S. Navy. He served until 1975 and again left with an honorable discharge. Public records show he reached pay grade E-5, which is a petty officer second class. They show a tour in Vietnam and two service medals. That is a real record of service, and many veterans in his audience respected it.

Cooper later told a bigger story. He said that in the early 1970s he served on an intelligence briefing team for the commander of the U.S. Pacific Fleet. In that job, he said, he read top-secret papers about UFOs and a secret group called MJ-12. This is a *claim*, a statement someone says is true. It is different from a *record*, which is evidence written down at the time by someone else.

Here the two do not match. The public records confirm Navy service but not a place on an intelligence team. A petty officer at pay grade E-5 was a skilled enlisted sailor, not a senior officer. Historians say that makes top-secret intelligence access unlikely, though not impossible. No document yet released places him on such a team. So the service is *documented*. The intelligence job is disputed.

words.d: a statement that someone says is true
evidence written down at the time, often by someone other than the person it describes
shown by records that other people can find and check
a military rank level that sets pay; E-5 is a mid-level enlisted rank

look.title: Record and Claim Side by Side
look.text: Column A, public Navy records: served until 1975; pay grade E-5; Vietnam tour; two service medals; honorable discharge. Column B, Cooper's later account: served on an intelligence briefing team for the Pacific Fleet commander in the early 1970s; read top-secret UFO papers.
look.prompt: Which items in Column B are also supported by Column A? Which stand only on Cooper's word? Write one fair sentence that describes his Navy service.

check.q: What do public records show about Cooper's Navy service?
choices: He was an admiral in the Pacific Fleet
He reached pay grade E-5, served in Vietnam and was honorably discharged
check.why: The reading lists E-5, a Vietnam tour, two service medals and an honorable discharge in 1975.

check.q: Which part of Cooper's Navy story is disputed?
choices: That he served in the Navy
That he served on a top-secret intelligence briefing team
check.why: The records confirm Navy service, Vietnam and the discharge. No released document places him on an intelligence team.

check.q: How is a record different from a claim?
choices: A record is evidence written down at the time; a claim is what someone says is true
A claim must be signed by an officer
check.why: The reading defines a claim as a statement someone says is true and a record as evidence written down at the time.

lessons.title: Weighing a Veteran's Word
lessons.mainIdea: A fair judge of Cooper's intelligence story lists the best evidence for it and against it before deciding how far it can be trusted.
reading: Many of Cooper's listeners believed his intelligence story because he told it with confidence and detail. That respect is worth taking seriously. Veterans often cannot prove what they did, because some duties were never written down in public files. A fair reader starts by asking what evidence would help, not by assuming the speaker is lying.

Here is the case for his story. His service in the Pacific was real. Briefing teams of the kind he described did exist. He told the story many times over many years. Here is the case against it. No document places him on such a team. His rank makes top-secret access unlikely. His story grew after the MJ-12 papers appeared in public in 1987. Some former colleagues in UFO research later broke with him and questioned his account.

When evidence runs out, historians use careful words. They do not say false, because nothing proves he never saw such papers. They do not say true, because nothing confirms it. They say *unproven* and they explain what is missing. They also watch for *corroboration*, meaning a second, independent source that backs up the first. Cooper's intelligence story has none so far. Released military files, if any exist, could still change the picture.

words.d: not shown true or false by the evidence we have
a second, independent source that backs up the first
a source that did not get its information from the first one

look.title: Three Ways to Say It
look.text: Sentence 1: Cooper lied about working in naval intelligence. Sentence 2: Cooper worked in naval intelligence and saw UFO papers. Sentence 3: Cooper said he worked in naval intelligence; no released record confirms it, and his rank makes it unlikely.
look.prompt: Which sentence claims only what the evidence supports? What new evidence would you need before you could write Sentence 1 or Sentence 2?

check.q: Which is part of the case FOR Cooper's intelligence story?
choices: His service in the Pacific was real
A document places him on the team
check.why: The reading lists real Pacific service, real briefing teams and a consistent retelling as the case for it.

check.q: What does corroboration mean?
choices: A second, independent source that backs up the first
A story told many times by the same person
check.why: Corroboration is support from a second source that did not get its information from the first.

check.q: Why do historians call the intelligence story unproven rather than false?
choices: Because nothing proves he never saw such papers, and nothing confirms that he did
Because all veterans' stories are true
check.why: Unproven means the evidence does not settle it either way, and the reading explains what is missing on both sides.

lessons.title: The MJ-12 Lectures
lessons.mainIdea: In 1988 and 1989 Cooper began telling the public about MJ-12, a secret committee that the FBI and Air Force investigators said was never formed.
reading: In 1988 Cooper began posting his story on ParaNet, a *bulletin board*. A bulletin board was an early online system where people dialed in by computer to read and post messages. Soon he was giving public lectures. A paper he wrote, dated 23 May 1989, was titled The Secret Government: The Origin, Identity, and Purpose of MJ-12. It told of alien contact and a hidden committee that managed it.

Cooper did not invent the name MJ-12. In December 1984 a TV producer named Jaime Shandera received undeveloped film in the mail. When printed, it showed a supposed top-secret briefing for President Eisenhower about a committee called Majestic 12. The pages were published in 1987. In 1988 the FBI began looking into them.

In September 1988 an agent of the Air Force Office of Special Investigations contacted the FBI about the papers. In November 1988 the Air Force investigators said no such committee had ever been authorized or formed. An FBI official called the document bogus. Cooper took an unusual position. He said the Shandera papers were *disinformation*, false material spread on purpose. Yet he still held that MJ-12 itself was real. That leaves his claim resting on his own memory of papers no one else has produced.

words.d: an early online system where people dialed in by computer to read and post messages
false information spread on purpose to mislead
short for Majestic 12, a supposed secret committee on UFOs described in disputed papers

look.title: The FBI's Majestic 12 File
look.text: In its file on the Majestic 12 papers, the FBI records that the Air Force Office of Special Investigations reported in late 1988 that no such committee had ever been authorized or formed. An FBI official judged the document to be completely fake.
look.cite: Federal Bureau of Investigation, Majestic 12 file, FBI Records: The Vault (records of 1988)
look.prompt: The FBI file judges the Shandera papers. Does it also settle Cooper's claim, which rests on papers he said he saw years earlier? Explain.

check.q: What was ParaNet?
check.why: The reading says Cooper first posted his story on ParaNet, an early online bulletin board.

check.q: What did Air Force investigators tell the FBI about MJ-12 in 1988?
choices: That it was real but secret
That no such committee had ever been authorized or formed
That it was run by the Navy
That Cooper had been a member
check.why: The FBI file records that the investigators said no such committee was ever authorized or formed.

check.q: What was unusual about Cooper's position on the Shandera papers?
choices: He called them disinformation but still said MJ-12 was real
He said they proved everything he claimed
check.why: Cooper called the published papers disinformation while holding that the committee itself existed.

lessons.title: Behold a Pale Horse
lessons.mainIdea: Cooper's 1991 book gathered lectures, reprinted documents and essays to argue that a secret society steers world events.
reading: In 1991 Light Technology Publishing in Arizona printed Cooper's book Behold a Pale Horse. The title comes from the Book of Revelation in the Bible, where a rider on a pale horse brings death. The title told readers that Cooper saw his subject as a warning about the end of an age.

The book is an *anthology*, a collection of separate pieces bound together. It holds Cooper's lectures, essays and many reprinted documents. Its main *thesis*, or central argument, is that a secret society he called the Illuminati steers world events. In his telling it works through governments, banks, private clubs and fraternal orders such as the Freemasons.

Because it is a collection, the book mixes very different materials. Some pieces point to real events that official records confirm. Others are documents with no known author or archive. One is a manual called Silent Weapons for Quiet Wars. The book says it was found in a used copier bought at a surplus sale. No author, agency or earlier copy has been traced. Historians treat the book as a *primary source* for what many Americans believed in the 1990s. They do not treat it as proof of the events it describes.

words.d: a collection of separate writings bound together in one book
the central argument of a book or essay
a document or object made at the time by someone involved

look.title: Three Kinds of Items
look.text: Item 1: a piece pointing to a government secret that official records, such as a 1977 Senate hearing, confirm. Item 2: a manual said to have been found in a surplus copier, with no known author or archive. Item 3: a reprint of a text that a London newspaper proved was copied from an 1864 French satire.
look.prompt: All three sit in the same book. Should a reader trust or reject the whole book at once, or judge each item? Explain your method.

check.q: Where does the title Behold a Pale Horse come from?
choices: The Book of Revelation in the Bible
check.why: The reading says the title comes from the Book of Revelation, where a rider on a pale horse brings death.

check.q: What is the book's main thesis?
choices: That a secret society Cooper called the Illuminati steers world events
That the Navy should be disbanded
check.why: The reading says the central argument is that a secret society he called the Illuminati steers world events.

check.q: How do historians use Behold a Pale Horse today?
choices: As proof of the events it describes
As a primary source for what many Americans believed in the 1990s
check.why: Historians read it as evidence of 1990s beliefs, not as proof of the events it describes.

lessons.title: The Hour of the Time
lessons.mainIdea: Cooper's shortwave program The Hour of the Time reached listeners across the country and made him a leading voice of the 1990s militia movement.
reading: In the 1990s Cooper hosted a radio program called The Hour of the Time. It was carried on WWCR, a *shortwave* station in Nashville, Tennessee. Shortwave radio uses signals that bounce off the upper atmosphere. At night they can travel across a whole continent. A cheap receiver was enough to listen, and no one needed a computer or a subscription.

The early 1990s were a time of deep distrust for many rural Americans. In 1992 a standoff at Ruby Ridge, Idaho, left a U.S. marshal and two members of the Weaver family dead. In 1993 the siege at Waco, Texas, ended in a fire, and more than 70 people died. Many listeners saw these as proof that the government would turn on its own citizens.

Cooper became a leading voice of the *militia movement*, armed private groups that saw the federal government as a threat. His *audience* was wide. It included truckers, farmers, veterans and people in prison. Many said he was the first person who took their fears seriously. That trust is part of the story historians try to understand, not something to mock.

words.d: radio signals that bounce off the upper atmosphere and can travel very long distances at night
armed private groups of the 1990s that saw the federal government as a threat
the people who listen to, watch or read something

look.title: Why Radio at Night?
look.text: A farmer in Montana, a trucker in Kansas and a man in a prison cell in Texas each turn on a small shortwave set after dark. None of them has internet access. The same voice reaches all three at once, with no editor between the speaker and the listener.
look.prompt: What made shortwave radio a strong tool for a speaker like Cooper? What checks that exist in a newspaper are missing on a live broadcast?

check.q: Why could Cooper's show reach listeners across the country at night?
choices: Shortwave signals bounce off the upper atmosphere and travel far
It was shown on national TV
It was printed in every newspaper
It needed a fast internet connection
check.why: The reading explains that shortwave signals bounce off the upper air and can cross a continent at night.

check.q: Which two events deepened distrust among many of Cooper's listeners?
choices: The Church Committee and the Rockefeller Commission
check.why: The reading names the 1992 Ruby Ridge standoff and the 1993 Waco siege.

check.q: What was the militia movement?
choices: Armed private groups that saw the federal government as a threat
check.why: The reading defines the militia movement as armed private groups of the 1990s that saw the federal government as a threat.

lessons.title: The 1998 Federal Charges
lessons.mainIdea: In 1998 Cooper was charged with tax evasion and bank fraud; he refused to surrender and was never tried.
reading: In 1998 federal authorities in Arizona charged Cooper with *tax evasion* and bank fraud. Tax evasion means illegally avoiding paying taxes that are owed. The charges came from a federal grand jury. The exact counts in the charging papers have not been checked for this course, so this lesson names only the two kinds of charge.

An *indictment* is a formal charge by a grand jury. It says there is enough evidence for a trial. It is not a finding of guilt. Cooper was never tried on these charges, so no court ever ruled on them. A fair account says he was charged, not that he was convicted.

Cooper did not surrender. He stayed at his home in Eagar, a small town in the White Mountains of eastern Arizona, and said he would not be taken. He became a *fugitive*, a person running from the law. According to a 2002 report by the Southern Poverty Law Center, federal agents put off serving his arrest warrant for more than three years. They wanted to avoid a violent confrontation like Ruby Ridge or Waco.

words.d: illegally avoiding paying taxes that are owed
a formal charge by a grand jury saying there is enough evidence for a trial
a person who is running from or refusing to surrender to the law

look.title: Charged Is Not Convicted
look.text: Headline A: Radio host guilty of tax crimes. Headline B: Radio host charged with tax evasion and bank fraud; refuses to surrender. Headline C: Government invents charges to silence radio host.
look.prompt: Which headline matches the facts in this lesson? What would a reporter need before writing Headline A or Headline C?

check.q: What was Cooper charged with in 1998?
check.why: Federal authorities charged him with tax evasion and bank fraud in 1998.

check.q: What is an indictment?
choices: A formal charge saying there is enough evidence for a trial
check.why: An indictment is a grand jury's formal charge. It is not a finding of guilt.

check.q: Why did federal agents put off serving Cooper's warrant, according to the SPLC report?
choices: They wanted to avoid a violent confrontation
check.why: The SPLC report says agents delayed for more than three years to avoid a violent confrontation.

lessons.title: Eagar, November 2001
lessons.mainIdea: On the night of 5 November 2001, a deputy was shot and badly wounded while trying to arrest Cooper, and another deputy's return fire killed Cooper.
reading: In July 2001, after a dispute with a local man, Arizona brought state charges against Cooper: aggravated assault with a deadly weapon, and endangerment. The details of that dispute have not been confirmed for this course. These charges were separate from the federal tax case. They were local, and they were handled by the Apache County Sheriff's Office.

On the night of 5 November 2001, a team of about 17 officers went to Cooper's home in Eagar to arrest him on the state charges. By the official account, Cooper shot Deputy Robert Marinez in the head. Marinez survived but was badly hurt. Another deputy returned fire and killed Cooper. He was 58 years old. Some sources give the date as 6 November, because the shooting came close to midnight.

Two accounts of that night still circulate. The official account comes from the sheriff's office and an investigation by the Arizona Department of Public Safety. Some of Cooper's supporters tell a different story. They say he was killed to silence him. A careful reader asks which *account* rests on records. The official file is a public record that can be requested. The silencing claim has no document behind it. It also has to explain why agents had avoided arresting him on the federal charges for years.

words.d: a description of an event from one person's or group's point of view
a serious attack or threat of attack, such as one made with a weapon
a government document that citizens can ask to see

look.title: Two Accounts of One Night
look.text: Account 1: Deputies came to arrest Cooper on a local assault charge. Cooper fired first and wounded a deputy. Another deputy fired back. Account 2: The government had waited for its chance to silence a man who knew too much.
look.prompt: For each account, list what evidence it rests on. What records would you request to test them?

check.q: What charges were deputies trying to arrest Cooper on in November 2001?
choices: Charges of spying for a foreign power
State charges of aggravated assault and endangerment
check.why: The deputies came on the July 2001 state charges, which were separate from the federal tax case.

check.q: What happened to Deputy Robert Marinez?
choices: He was shot in the head and survived
He arrested Cooper without a fight
check.why: The reading says Marinez was shot in the head, was badly hurt and survived.

check.q: Which fact is hard for the silencing claim to explain?
choices: Agents had avoided arresting him on the federal charges for years
check.why: If the goal was to silence him, the long delay in serving the federal warrant is hard to explain.

lessons.title: An Audience That Kept Growing
lessons.mainIdea: Cooper's influence grew after his death, and his biographer links it to a wider loss of public trust in American institutions.
reading: Cooper's death did not end his influence. Recordings of The Hour of the Time were copied and shared, first on tapes and then online. Behold a Pale Horse stayed in print for decades. Reporters have found it passed hand to hand in prisons and quoted in hip-hop culture and online movements. Its readers include people of many backgrounds and politics.

The journalist Mark Jacobson wrote the first full *biography* of Cooper, Pale Horse Rider, published in 2018. A biography is the story of a person's life written by someone else. Jacobson interviewed Cooper's family, fellow broadcasters and longtime listeners. He tried to explain why so many people trusted Cooper more than they trusted their government.

Scholars add another angle. The legal scholar Mark Fenster argues that belief in conspiracy is often a response to real *secrecy* and real distrust, not simple foolishness. Secrecy means keeping information hidden from people who might want it. Cooper's audience had real reasons for distrust, as the next section shows. The hard question is what to do with that distrust. It can lead a person to demand records, or it can lead a person to believe anything that sounds defiant.

words.d: the story of a person's life written by someone else
keeping information hidden from people who might want it
the power to shape what other people think or do

look.title: A Scholar on Why People Believe
look.text: Fenster argues that conspiracy theories are not simply mistakes by foolish people. He treats them as a response to real secrecy and real inequalities of power, and as a way people try to make sense of a political order they do not trust.
look.cite: Mark Fenster, Conspiracy Theories: Secrecy and Power in American Culture (University of Minnesota Press, 1999; rev. 2008)
look.prompt: How does Fenster's view change the way a student might talk with a friend who admires Cooper?

check.q: Who wrote the full biography Pale Horse Rider (2018)?
check.why: Journalist Mark Jacobson wrote Pale Horse Rider after interviewing family, broadcasters and listeners.

check.q: What does Mark Fenster argue about conspiracy belief?
choices: It is often a response to real secrecy and distrust
It is always a sign of foolishness
It only appears on shortwave radio
check.why: Fenster treats conspiracy belief as a response to real secrecy and distrust, not simple foolishness.

check.q: According to the reading, where has Behold a Pale Horse been passed around?
choices: In prisons, hip-hop culture and online movements
check.why: The reading says reporters found it in prisons and in hip-hop culture and online movements.

lessons.title: What the Records Confirm
lessons.mainIdea: Several things Cooper talked about are documented: MKUltra, COINTELPRO, Operation Northwoods, and real elite groups such as the Bohemian Grove, the CFR and the Trilateral Commission.
reading: A *ledger* is a book of accounts with columns. Historians borrow the idea to sort claims. The first column holds what official records confirm. Cooper deserves credit here. He told a mass audience to take government secrecy seriously, and some of the secrets were real.

The CIA's MKUltra program, approved in 1953, secretly tested drugs such as LSD on people who did not know. The FBI's COINTELPRO, from 1956 to 1971, spied on and tried to disrupt American political groups. Both came fully to light in the 1970s through the press and Congress, including the Church Committee report of 1976. In 1962 the Joint Chiefs of Staff proposed Operation Northwoods, a plan to stage attacks and blame Cuba. President Kennedy's administration rejected it.

Some groups Cooper named are also real. The Bohemian Club, founded in San Francisco in 1872, gathers powerful men each July at the Bohemian Grove in California. The Council on Foreign Relations was founded in New York in 1921. The Trilateral Commission was founded in 1973 by David Rockefeller. All three have members in high office. Their existence is documented. That they secretly run the world is a separate claim, and the records do not show it.

words.d: a book of accounts in columns; here, a chart that sorts claims by evidence
a CIA program begun in 1953 that secretly tested drugs on people, some without their knowledge
the FBI's secret program, 1956 to 1971, to spy on and disrupt American political groups
a 1962 Joint Chiefs proposal to stage attacks and blame Cuba; it was rejected

look.title: When Could Cooper Have Known?
look.cite: U.S. Senate, Project MKULTRA joint hearing (1977); Church Committee Final Report (1976); JFK Assassination Records Review Board release (1997)
look.prompt: The Northwoods memo became public six years after the book. What does that tell you about the difference between a guess that later looks right and a claim backed by evidence at the time?

check.q: What was MKUltra?
choices: An FBI program against civil rights groups
A 1962 plan to stage attacks on Cuba
A CIA program that secretly tested drugs on people
check.why: MKUltra, approved in 1953, was the CIA program that tested drugs such as LSD on people who did not know.

check.q: What happened to Operation Northwoods?
check.why: The Joint Chiefs proposed it in 1962, and the Kennedy administration rejected it.

check.q: Which statement about the Council on Foreign Relations is documented?
choices: It was founded in 1921 and has members in high office
It was founded by Bill Cooper
It meets each July at the Bohemian Grove
check.why: The group's founding and membership are documented. The claim that it runs the world is not.

lessons.title: Disputed and Unproven Claims
lessons.mainIdea: Cooper's claims about MJ-12, a treaty with aliens, Kennedy's assassination and a single shadow government lack the records needed to prove them.
reading: The second column of the ledger holds claims that are disputed or unproven. Cooper said MJ-12 was a real committee formed to handle crashed alien craft. The only papers ever produced were judged fake by Air Force investigators, and Cooper himself rejected them. He also said President Eisenhower met aliens in 1954 and signed a treaty with them. No document, witness record or budget line supports that. In 2024 a Defense Department office reviewed the record and found no evidence of agreements with aliens.

Cooper said the Secret Service driver of Kennedy's car, William Greer, fired the fatal shot in Dallas in 1963. He pointed to a flash in a copy of the Zapruder film. Researchers who studied clearer copies found no gun. A congressional medical panel in the late 1970s found the wounds came from behind and above. Some historians still debate whether Lee Harvey Oswald acted alone, but the driver theory is not part of that serious debate.

Cooper's biggest claim was a *shadow government*, one hidden group that runs the country behind the elected one. Real cases of hidden programs exist, such as MKUltra and the Iran-Contra affair of the 1980s. But each was exposed by Congress, the press, courts or *whistleblowers*. Historians see many separate secrets, not one master plan. That is why the big claim stays unproven.

words.d: a supposed hidden group that secretly runs a country behind its elected leaders
an insider who reports wrongdoing to the public or to officials
argued over, with serious people on different sides

look.title: Small Secrets and One Big Plan
look.text: Claim A: The CIA hid a drug-testing program from the public in the 1950s. Claim B: One hidden group has secretly controlled the U.S. government for decades. Claim A has a 1977 Senate hearing and surviving CIA financial records. Claim B points to Claim A as its proof.
look.prompt: Does proving Claim A also prove Claim B? Explain the gap between them in your own words.

check.q: What did a 2024 Defense Department review find about agreements with aliens?
choices: It found no evidence of any such agreement
It said the records were destroyed
check.why: The reading says the 2024 review found no evidence of agreements with aliens.

check.q: Why is the claim about Kennedy's driver not part of the serious debate?
choices: Clearer film copies show no gun, and medical findings point to shots from behind
check.why: Researchers found no gun on clearer copies, and a medical panel found the wounds came from behind and above.

check.q: Why do historians call the shadow-government claim unproven?
choices: Real hidden programs were separate and were exposed, which does not show one master group
check.why: Historians see many separate secrets that came to light, not one hidden ruler behind them all.

lessons.title: Shown False: A Forgery and a Spoof
lessons.mainIdea: Two items in Cooper's book are shown false: the Protocols of the Elders of Zion, a proven antisemitic forgery, and Alternative 3, a TV spoof.
reading: The third column holds claims shown false. The first is the Protocols of the Elders of Zion. The 1991 edition of Behold a Pale Horse reprinted it as a full chapter. The Protocols claim to be secret plans of Jewish leaders to rule the world. In 1921 Philip Graves showed in The Times of London that whole passages were copied from an 1864 French satire by Maurice Joly. That satire attacked Napoleon III and never mentioned Jews. It was a *forgery*, and it has fed hatred and violence against Jewish people for more than a century.

Scholars such as Michael Barkun report that Cooper added a note before the chapter. It told readers to read the word Illuminati wherever the text said Jews. That swap does not repair the text. It is a forgery whatever word is put in, and it was written to accuse Jews. The swap keeps the forgery in circulation. Later revised printings of the book reportedly dropped the chapter, but this has not been confirmed from the publisher.

The second false item is Alternative 3. On 20 June 1977 Anglia Television in Britain aired a program that looked like a documentary about a secret colony on Mars. It was a *spoof*, a made-up program in the style of a real one. It was written by David Ambrose, meant for April Fools' Day and credited its actors. Cooper's book repeated its plot as fact. A fair reader can say both things at once: Cooper raised real questions about power, and his book also passed on a known forgery and a known spoof.

words.d: a document falsely made to look like the real work of someone else
showing hatred of or prejudice against Jewish people
a made-up program or text in the style of a real one, made as a joke or hoax
writing that mocks a person or government, often by exaggeration

look.title: A Scholar Reads the Swap
look.text: Barkun describes Cooper's note, which asked readers to substitute Illuminati for Jews in the Protocols, as a key example of how conspiracy writers of the 1990s blended UFO lore with much older conspiracy stories, including a known antisemitic forgery.
look.cite: Michael Barkun, A Culture of Conspiracy: Apocalyptic Visions in Contemporary America (University of California Press, 2003)
look.prompt: Why does changing one word not change what the Protocols are? Use the word forgery in your answer.

check.q: What did Philip Graves show in 1921?
choices: That the Protocols copied passages from an 1864 satire by Maurice Joly
check.why: Graves showed in The Times of London that the Protocols copied whole passages from Joly's 1864 satire.

check.q: Why does swapping Illuminati for Jews not fix the Protocols?
choices: The text is a forgery whatever word is used, and it was written to accuse Jews
Because the Illuminati never existed at all
Because Cooper wrote the swap himself
check.why: The reading says the text is a forgery whatever word is swapped in, and the swap keeps it in circulation.

check.q: What was Alternative 3?
choices: A 1977 British TV spoof about a secret Mars colony
A chapter of the Church Committee report
check.why: Anglia Television aired it in 1977. It was a scripted spoof with credited actors.

review.q: Which part of Cooper's life is best documented by public records?
choices: His place on a Navy intelligence briefing team
His honorable service in the Air Force and Navy
review.why: Public records confirm his Air Force and Navy service and honorable discharges. The intelligence job is disputed.

review.q: What kind of book is Behold a Pale Horse?
choices: An anthology of lectures, essays and reprinted documents
review.why: The book gathers Cooper's lectures, essays and many reprinted documents.

review.q: Which claim belongs in the documented column of the ledger?
choices: The FBI ran COINTELPRO to spy on and disrupt political groups
Eisenhower signed a treaty with aliens
review.why: COINTELPRO is confirmed by FBI files and the Church Committee report.

review.q: Which claim belongs in the shown-false column?
choices: The Trilateral Commission was founded in 1973
The Protocols are a genuine secret plan
review.why: The Protocols were proven a forgery, copied from Joly's 1864 satire.

review.q: Why does the Northwoods memo not show that Cooper had evidence for it in 1991?
choices: It was released in 1997, after his book
review.why: The memo was released in 1997, six years after the book was published.

review.q: On what charges were deputies trying to arrest Cooper in 2001?
choices: State charges of aggravated assault and endangerment
review.why: The 2001 arrest attempt was on state charges from a July 2001 dispute.

review.q: How did Cooper treat the MJ-12 papers that Jaime Shandera received?
choices: He sent them to the FBI
He said they proved the alien treaty
He called them disinformation but still said MJ-12 was real
review.why: Cooper rejected the Shandera papers as disinformation while holding that the committee existed.

review.q: Which statement is the fairest summary of Cooper's ledger?
choices: Only his claims about aliens were wrong
Some claims are documented, many are unproven, and some are shown false
review.why: The ledger sorts his claims into three columns: documented, disputed or unproven, and shown false.

chapters.title: Capstone: Test a Claim
chapters.bigQuestion: How do you test a claim you already believe, and what do you owe the people who disagree with your answer?

story.title: The Eye on the Dollar
story.kicker: A high school senior sets out to prove something she has believed since middle school, and the evidence takes her somewhere she did not expect.
paragraphs: Maya is a senior at a high school outside Chicago. Since seventh grade she has believed one thing for certain. The eye above the pyramid on the back of the dollar bill is a secret sign of the Illuminati. A cousin showed her a video about it years ago. For her capstone project, she decides to prove it once and for all.

She starts where her teacher told her to start: with the earliest source. That leads her to a report written on 20 August 1776 by the first committee Congress asked to design a national seal. The report proposes an Eye of Providence in a triangle, a common Christian image of God watching over people. The idea came from an artist hired by the committee. No record shows he was ever a Freemason or a member of any secret order.

Then she checks the Illuminati. The order was founded on 1 May 1776 in Bavaria, in what is now Germany. That is the same year. For a moment she feels sure she has found her proof. Then she reads further. The eye and pyramid were adopted on the seal in 1782 and first printed on the dollar in 1935. No document links anyone who designed the seal to the Bavarian order.

Maya does not throw out her whole question. She sorts it. Some parts are documented. Some are only coincidence. Some have no evidence at all. Her final paper is not the one she planned to write, and she is proud of it. In this chapter you will follow the same steps with a claim of your own.
story.think: Maya felt sure for a moment when she found the same year, 1776. Why is a matching date not the same as a connection?

sections.title: Choose a Claim and Trace It

lessons.title: Pick a Claim You Can Test
lessons.mainIdea: A good capstone claim is narrow and specific enough that evidence could show it true or false.
reading: Compare two claims. The first says the Illuminati control everything. The second says the eye on the dollar bill was put there by the Illuminati. The first is too big to test. Any event can be fitted into it, and no single record could ever answer it. The second names one object, one group and one action. Records can speak to it.

Historians call a claim like the second one *testable*. A testable claim is one that evidence could, in principle, support or undercut. A useful habit is to ask: what would I expect to find if this were true, and what would I expect to find if it were false? If the answer is the same either way, the claim cannot be tested as written.

To make a big claim testable, *narrow* it. Pick one society, one document, one event or one date. Good examples from this course include the Templars and banking, Prince Hall's first lodge, the Washington letters about the Illuminati, the Protocols, the MJ-12 papers and Bill Cooper's Navy service. Choose a claim you care about. You will work harder on a question that matters to you, even if the answer surprises you.

words.d: able to be supported or undercut by evidence
to make a question smaller and more specific
a final project that brings together the skills of a whole course

look.title: Too Big, Just Right
look.text: Claim 1: Secret societies run the world. Claim 2: Freemasons shaped the American Revolution. Claim 3: Prince Hall and other free Black men were made Masons in Boston in 1775.
look.prompt: Rank the three claims from hardest to easiest to test. Rewrite Claim 1 or Claim 2 so that a single record could help answer it.

check.q: Which claim is testable as written?
choices: The eye on the dollar bill was put there by the Illuminati
Powerful people always hide the truth
check.why: It names one object, one group and one action, so records can speak to it.

check.q: What question helps you tell whether a claim is testable?
choices: What would I expect to find if it were true, and if it were false?
Is it about a famous person?
check.why: If you would expect the same evidence either way, the claim cannot be tested as written.

check.q: How do you make a big claim testable?
choices: Narrow it to one society, document, event or date
check.why: Narrowing a claim to one specific thing lets records answer it.

lessons.title: Find the Earliest Source
lessons.mainIdea: Tracing a claim back to its earliest known source often shows where it began and whether any evidence ever stood behind it.
reading: Most claims reach us secondhand. A video repeats a book. The book repeats an article. The article repeats a pamphlet. Each copy can add details and drop warnings. So a careful researcher works backward, one step at a time, looking for the *origin*, the first known appearance of a claim.

Tracing the origin can settle a great deal. The story of the Priory of Sion, a supposed medieval order, traces back to typed pages deposited in France's national library in 1967. Its makers later admitted they invented it. In another case from this course, a popular story says the Knights Templar gave pilgrims letters of credit from about 1150. Researchers for this course found that date only on popular websites. Scholarly sources confirm that the Templars moved money over long distances, but not that exact story.

The earliest source is not always right, and a late source is not always wrong. But the origin tells you what the first teller knew, and when. Record each step in a *source chain*, a list of who repeated the claim, when, and where they got it. A gap in the chain is a clue. It is often where a guess turned into a fact.

words.d: the first known appearance of a claim or story
a list of who repeated a claim, when, and where they got it
heard or read from someone else rather than seen directly

look.title: Build a Source Chain
look.text: A 2024 video says the Templars invented the bank check. The video cites a 2010 website. The website cites a 1990s popular history book. That book gives no footnote. Scholarly histories of the Templars describe money transfers between their houses but do not mention pilgrims' letters of credit.
look.prompt: Draw the chain from the video back as far as it goes. Where does the evidence stop? What would you look for next?

check.q: What is the origin of a claim?
choices: The most popular version of it
The version with the most detail
The first known appearance of it
check.why: The reading defines origin as the first known appearance of a claim.

check.q: Where did the Priory of Sion story trace back to?
choices: Typed pages deposited in France's national library in 1967
check.why: The story began with pages deposited in 1967, which their makers later admitted they invented.

check.q: Why is a gap in a source chain a useful clue?
choices: It proves the claim is true
It shows the claim is very old
It is often where a guess turned into a fact
It means the claim was never repeated
check.why: The reading says a gap is often the place where a guess became treated as fact.

lessons.title: Who Made It, and Why?
lessons.mainIdea: Asking who first made a claim, for what audience and with what purpose helps a researcher judge how much weight it can bear.
reading: Every source has an author, an audience and a purpose. The *author* is who made it. The audience is who it was made for. The *purpose* is what it was meant to do: inform, persuade, entertain, sell or attack. None of these alone makes a claim true or false. Together they tell you what questions to ask.

Take the so-called Knights of Columbus oath. In the early 1900s anti-Catholic activists spread a text they said was the secret oath of that Catholic fraternal order. It described violent promises. In 1913 a committee of the U.S. House of Representatives looked at it during a disputed election case. The committee condemned the text as false and libelous. Its purpose had been to make voters fear Catholic candidates.

Purpose matters most when a claim targets a whole group. The Protocols of the Elders of Zion first appeared in a Russian newspaper in 1903, at a time of violent attacks on Jews in the Russian Empire. The Knights of Columbus oath appeared during a wave of anti-Catholic politics. In both cases the *motive* helps explain why a false text was made and why people wanted to believe it. Most Catholics and Jews, of course, had nothing to do with any plot at all.

words.d: the person or group who made a source
what a source was meant to do, such as inform, persuade or attack
the reason a person has for doing something
falsely damaging someone's reputation in writing

look.title: Congress Judges a Fake Oath
look.text: A House elections committee reviewing a contested election strongly condemned the publication of the so-called Knights of Columbus oath. It called the oath spurious and the article false and libelous.
look.cite: U.S. House, Committee on Elections No. 1, report in Bonniwell v. Butler, Congressional Record, 15 February 1913
look.prompt: Who made the fake oath, and what was its purpose? Why does an official committee's finding carry weight here?

check.q: What is the purpose of a source?
choices: What it was meant to do, such as inform, persuade or attack
The number of pages it has
check.why: The reading defines purpose as what a source was meant to do.

check.q: What did a House committee decide about the Knights of Columbus oath in 1913?
choices: It should be taught in schools
check.why: The committee condemned the text as false and libelous.

check.q: Where did the Protocols first appear?
check.why: The Protocols were first printed in a Russian newspaper in 1903. The London Times exposed them in 1921.

sections.title: Gather Evidence From More Than One Side

lessons.title: Documents and Archives
lessons.mainIdea: Original documents kept in archives are the strongest evidence, because anyone can go back and check them.
reading: An *archive* is a place that keeps original records so people can study them later. The National Archives in Washington holds the founding documents of the United States. Libraries, courthouses, churches and lodges keep archives too. A document in an archive has a known home, and other researchers can check the same page you read.

Maya's strongest evidence came from archives. The first seal committee's report of 20 August 1776 survives. It describes the Eye of Providence in a triangle. The final design of the Great Seal, with the eye above the pyramid, was adopted on 20 June 1782. Government records show the seal's reverse was added to the dollar bill in 1935. Each step has a date and a document.

An archive does not make a document true. In chapter 30 you saw that the Dossiers Secrets sat in France's national library and were still a hoax. What an archive gives you is *provenance*, the known history of where a document came from and who held it. A record with a long, clear provenance is far stronger than one that appears from nowhere, like film in a mailbox or a manual in a used copier.

words.d: a place that keeps original records so people can study them later
the known history of where a document came from and who has held it
the official seal of the United States, adopted in 1782, used to mark government documents

look.title: The Eye and the Pyramid: A Paper Trail
rows: First seal committee proposes the eye
Seal's reverse printed on the $1 bill
look.cite: U.S. National Archives, Original Design of the Great Seal; U.S. Department of State, The Great Seal of the United States
look.prompt: Two events share the year 1776. What would you need to find to show that one caused the other?

check.q: What is an archive?
choices: A place that keeps original records so people can study them
check.why: The reading defines an archive as a place that keeps original records for later study.

check.q: When was the Great Seal's design adopted?
check.why: The final design was adopted on 20 June 1782. The eye was first proposed in 1776.

check.q: Why does an archive not make a document true?
choices: A hoax like the Dossiers Secrets can still be placed in a library
check.why: The Dossiers Secrets sat in France's national library and were still a hoax. Archives give provenance, not proof.

lessons.title: Court Records and Official Inquiries
lessons.mainIdea: Courts and official inquiries test evidence under rules, so their findings are strong sources, though a researcher still reads them critically.
reading: Courts and official inquiries do something ordinary writers cannot. They can *subpoena* records, which means order people to hand them over. They hear witnesses under oath. They let the other side cross-examine. Their findings are written down and kept. That process makes their records among the strongest sources a researcher can use.

This course has used many. In 1934 and 1935 a court in Bern, Switzerland, heard a case about the Protocols and ruled on 14 May 1935 that they were a forgery. In 1976 the Senate's Church Committee published its final report on intelligence abuses, including COINTELPRO. In 1987 the Maxi Trial in Palermo convicted hundreds of Mafia members after years of investigation led by prosecutors Giovanni Falcone and Paolo Borsellino.

Read these records with care too. A court decides a narrow legal question, not every question. An inquiry may be limited by what records survived; the CIA had ordered most MKUltra files destroyed in 1973. And a charge is not a *verdict*. A verdict is a court's final decision on guilt. When you cite a court record, say what the court actually decided.

words.d: a legal order to hand over records or appear as a witness
a court's final decision on whether someone is guilty
an official investigation into what happened

look.title: What Did the Court Decide?
look.text: Student A writes: The Bern court proved that everything bad ever said about secret societies is false. Student B writes: In 1935 a court in Bern ruled that the Protocols were a forgery.
look.prompt: Which student cites the court record correctly? Explain what Student A did wrong.

check.q: What is a subpoena?
choices: A legal order to hand over records or appear as a witness
check.why: A subpoena orders people to hand over records or to testify.

check.q: What did the Bern court rule on 14 May 1935?
choices: That the Protocols were a forgery
That the Mafia did not exist
check.why: The Bern court ruled in 1935 that the Protocols were a forgery.

check.q: Why might an inquiry into MKUltra have limits?
choices: Most MKUltra files had been ordered destroyed in 1973
check.why: The reading says the CIA ordered most MKUltra files destroyed in 1973, which limited what could be studied.

lessons.title: Scholars Who Disagree
lessons.mainIdea: Serious scholars sometimes disagree about dates and facts, and a fair researcher reports each view and the evidence behind it.
reading: Scholars are experts who study a subject for years and publish their evidence for others to check. They do not always agree. When they disagree, a researcher does not pick the answer they like best. They report each view and the evidence behind it, so readers can judge for themselves.

Here are two examples from this course. Tradition says Prince Hall and fourteen other free Black men were made Masons in Boston on 6 March 1775. In 2026 the historian Oscar Alleyne presented a paper arguing that the date was 1778. Likewise, the first Grand Lodge of Freemasons in London is traditionally dated to 1717. Some historians argue for 1721, based on the earliest surviving records.

These are not fights between truth and lies. They are *scholarly debates*, where experts weigh the same kinds of evidence and reach different readings. A fair sentence names both: traditionally dated 1717, though some historians argue 1721. That kind of sentence shows your reader that you did the work. It also leaves room for new evidence, because *revision*, the updating of history as new records are found, is normal and healthy.

words.d: an expert who studies a subject for years and publishes evidence for others to check
a disagreement among experts who weigh evidence and reach different readings
updating a history as new records are found or old ones are reread

look.title: Write the Fair Sentence
look.text: Traditional date: Prince Hall and fourteen other free Black men made Masons in Boston, 6 March 1775. A 2026 paper by historian Oscar Alleyne: argues the date was 6 March 1778.
look.prompt: Write one sentence for your capstone that reports both views fairly without choosing between them. Then say what evidence could settle it.

check.q: What does a fair researcher do when scholars disagree?
choices: Picks the view they like best
Reports each view and the evidence behind it
check.why: The reading says a researcher reports each view and its evidence.

check.q: What date did Oscar Alleyne argue for Prince Hall's initiation?
check.why: Alleyne's 2026 paper argues for 1778. The traditional date is 1775.

check.q: What is revision in history?
choices: Updating a history as new records are found or reread
Copying a text word for word
check.why: Revision means updating history in light of new or reread evidence, which is normal and healthy.

lessons.title: When Numbers Disagree
lessons.mainIdea: When sources give different numbers for the same event, a careful researcher reports the range and names the sources.
reading: Sometimes sources give different numbers for the same thing. The Maxi Trial in Palermo, Italy, is a good example. The verdict came on 16 December 1987. Italian news accounts say 346 people were convicted and 114 were acquitted, with 19 life sentences. English Wikipedia gives 338 convictions. Other sites give numbers in between.

Differences like this usually have ordinary causes. Some sources count people charged at the start; others count only those still on trial at the verdict. Some count later appeals. Some copy an early news report that was later corrected. The first job is to find out what each number is counting.

When you cannot settle it, report a *range*: more than 330 people were convicted. Name your sources. Round when the exact figure is uncertain. Never pick the number that best fits your argument and hide the rest. Honest handling of numbers is part of *credibility*, the reason readers can trust you.

words.d: the span between the lowest and highest numbers the sources give
the quality that makes a writer or source worth trusting
found not guilty by a court

look.title: The Maxi Trial Verdict, 1987
look.cite: Italian press reports of the 16 December 1987 verdict (Il Sussidiario; Geopop); Italian Chamber of Deputies, Antimafia Commission chronology (114 acquitted, 19 life terms)
look.prompt: The convicted and acquitted add up to 460, not 475. What might explain the difference? How would you write the number in your paper?

check.q: What is one ordinary reason sources give different numbers?
choices: They count different things, such as people charged versus people still on trial
check.why: The reading says sources may count people charged, people at the verdict or later appeals.

check.q: How should you report a number you cannot settle?
choices: Pick the one that best fits your argument
Give a range and name your sources
check.why: The reading says to report a range, name sources and round when uncertain.

check.q: What does credibility mean?
choices: The quality that makes a writer or source worth trusting
The number of pages in a report
check.why: Credibility is the reason readers can trust a writer or source.

lessons.title: Three Piles of Evidence
lessons.mainIdea: Sort the parts of a claim into documented, disputed and unsupported, because most big claims mix all three.
reading: Few claims are wholly true or wholly false. Most bundle several smaller claims together. Your job is to pull them apart and sort each piece into one of three piles. You did this with Bill Cooper's ledger in chapter 33. Now you do it with your own claim.

*Documented* means records that others can check support it. *Disputed* means serious people read the evidence differently. *Unsupported* means no reliable evidence backs it, or strong evidence shows it false. Maya's claim broke into pieces. The eye appears on the dollar: documented. The eye was proposed in 1776: documented. The Illuminati were founded the same year: documented. Masons shaped the design: disputed at most, since one committee member, Benjamin Franklin, was a Mason and others, such as John Adams, were not. The Illuminati put the eye there: unsupported.

Notice what sorting does. It lets you agree with the true parts of a claim you are testing. It shows exactly where the evidence stops. And it keeps you from rejecting a whole claim because one piece is weak, or accepting a whole claim because one piece is strong. That is the heart of *critical thinking*.

words.d: supported by records that other people can find and check
read differently by serious people looking at the evidence
backed by no reliable evidence, or shown false by strong evidence
judging a claim by carefully weighing the evidence for each part

look.title: Sort Maya's Claim
look.text: Piece 1: The eye appears on the back of the dollar. Piece 2: The eye was proposed to Congress's seal committee in 1776. Piece 3: Benjamin Franklin, a Freemason, sat on that committee. Piece 4: The Illuminati designed the seal. Piece 5: The Illuminati were founded in 1776.
look.prompt: Put each piece into documented, disputed or unsupported. For each, name the kind of record that decided it.

check.q: What does disputed mean in the three-pile method?
choices: Serious people read the evidence differently
check.why: Disputed means serious people read the same evidence in different ways.

check.q: Which piece of Maya's claim is unsupported?
choices: The eye appears on the dollar
The Illuminati put the eye on the seal
check.why: No document links the seal's designers to the Illuminati, so that piece is unsupported.

check.q: Why is sorting a claim into pieces useful?
choices: It shows exactly where the evidence stops
It lets you skip the earliest source
check.why: Sorting lets you accept the true parts and see where the evidence runs out.

lessons.title: Build an Argument From Evidence
lessons.mainIdea: An argument from evidence states a claim, backs it with specific sources, explains the reasoning and answers the strongest counterclaim.
reading: An argument in history is not a shouting match. It is a careful case. It has four parts. The *claim* is your answer to the question. The evidence is the specific facts and sources that support it. The reasoning explains how the evidence supports the claim. The *counterclaim* is the strongest opposing view, which you state fairly and then answer.

Here is a short example. Claim: the eye on the dollar is not an Illuminati symbol. Evidence: a 1776 committee report proposes it as the Eye of Providence; the seal was adopted in 1782; no document links its designers to the Bavarian order. Reasoning: the record traces the image to a common Christian symbol, chosen by people with no known tie to the Illuminati. Counterclaim: both began in 1776. Answer: a shared year is a *coincidence* unless a record connects them.

The strongest arguments admit what they cannot prove. A writer who says the evidence does not settle this part earns more trust than one who claims to know everything. The historian Richard Hofstadter warned in 1964 against a style of argument that piles up facts toward one grand hidden plot. Your job is the opposite: let the evidence set the size of your claim.

words.d: in an argument, your answer to the question
the strongest opposing view, stated fairly
two things happening together by chance, with no cause linking them
the explanation of how the evidence supports the claim

look.title: A Historian on a Style of Argument
look.text: Hofstadter described a paranoid style in American politics, marked by heated exaggeration, deep suspicion and a sense of vast conspiracy. He argued that such writing often gathers many real facts but leaps from them to one hidden, all-powerful plot.
look.cite: Richard Hofstadter, The Paranoid Style in American Politics, Harper's Magazine, November 1964
look.prompt: Hofstadter says this style often uses real facts. Where exactly is the leap? How can the four-part argument help you avoid it?

check.q: What is a counterclaim?
choices: The strongest opposing view, stated fairly
check.why: A counterclaim is the best opposing view, which a strong argument states fairly and answers.

check.q: In the example argument, how is the shared year 1776 explained?
choices: As a mistake in the records
As a coincidence unless a record connects the two
check.why: The answer to the counterclaim says a shared year is a coincidence unless a record connects them.

check.q: What did Hofstadter warn against in 1964?
choices: Leaping from real facts to one grand hidden plot
check.why: Hofstadter described a style that piles up facts and leaps to one vast conspiracy.

lessons.title: Changing Your Mind Honestly
lessons.mainIdea: Changing a view when the evidence calls for it is a strength, and even George Washington separated what he believed from what he could show.
reading: Maya began her project sure of one answer and ended with another. That can feel like losing. It is not. Changing your mind because of evidence is called *intellectual honesty*. It means you care more about what is true than about being right. It is a sign of a strong thinker.

Historians do it too. In 2011 researchers cracked the Copiale Cipher, a coded book from a German secret society. They first dated it to about 1760 to 1780. Further study moved the date to about 1730. The researchers did not hide the change. They published it, and the history got better.

Even George Washington drew careful lines. In 1798 a minister named G. W. Snyder warned him that Illuminati ideas were spreading through American Masonic lodges. Washington wrote back twice. He said he did not doubt that Illuminati and radical French ideas had reached the United States. But he said he did not believe the lodges themselves were spreading them. He separated a general worry from a specific charge he had no evidence for. That is a model for your *conclusion*, the final judgment you reach from your evidence.

words.d: changing or keeping a view based on the evidence, not on wanting to be right
the final judgment you reach from your evidence
a code that replaces letters or words with other symbols

look.title: Washington Draws a Line
look.text: Washington told Snyder he had not meant to doubt that Illuminati and Jacobin ideas had spread in the United States; he was fully satisfied that they had. What he doubted was that the Masonic lodges, as societies, had worked to spread them.
look.cite: George Washington to G. W. Snyder, 24 October 1798, George Washington Papers, Library of Congress
look.prompt: What did Washington accept, and what did he refuse to accept without evidence? How is that like sorting a claim into piles?

check.q: What is intellectual honesty?
choices: Changing or keeping a view based on the evidence
check.why: Intellectual honesty means caring more about what is true than about being right.

check.q: How did researchers change the date of the Copiale Cipher?
check.why: They first dated it about 1760 to 1780, then moved it to about 1730 after further study.

check.q: What did Washington doubt in his 1798 letters?
choices: That the lodges, as societies, were spreading Illuminati ideas
That radical ideas had reached America
check.why: Washington accepted that the ideas had spread but doubted the lodges were spreading them.

lessons.title: Presenting Your Findings
lessons.mainIdea: A clear capstone presentation states the question, shows the source chain and the three piles, and ends with a conclusion the evidence can carry.
reading: Your *presentation* is how you share your work with others, by speaking, writing or both. A strong one follows the path you took. Start with the question and why it matters to you. Show the earliest source you found. Walk your listeners through the source chain. Then show your three piles, and end with your conclusion.

Show, do not just tell. Put the key document on a slide or a handout: a date, a title, a line or two in paraphrase. Name each source out loud with its author and year. A *citation* is a note that tells readers exactly where a fact came from, so they can check it. In a talk, a spoken citation works too, such as: according to the 1977 Senate hearing on MKUltra.

Keep it short and plain. One idea per slide. Use the course terms you have learned: provenance, corroboration, documented, disputed. Tell your listeners what surprised you. If your view changed, say so and say why. Listeners trust a speaker who shows the path, including the wrong turns.

words.d: sharing your work with others by speaking, writing or both
a note that tells readers exactly where a fact came from
a printed page given to listeners to follow along

look.title: Plan Five Slides
look.text: Slide 1: My question and why I chose it. Slide 2: The earliest source I found. Slide 3: My source chain. Slide 4: Documented, disputed, unsupported. Slide 5: My conclusion and what would change my mind.
look.prompt: Fill in one line for each slide using your own claim. Which slide was hardest to write, and why?

check.q: What is a citation?
choices: A note that tells readers exactly where a fact came from
check.why: A citation lets readers find and check the source of a fact.

check.q: According to the reading, how should a presentation end?
choices: With a conclusion the evidence can carry
With a list of every website visited
check.why: The reading says to end with a conclusion after showing the source chain and the three piles.

check.q: Why should you tell listeners if your view changed?
choices: Listeners trust a speaker who shows the path, including wrong turns
check.why: The reading says showing the whole path, including wrong turns, builds trust.

lessons.title: Disagreeing Without Contempt
lessons.mainIdea: Respectful disagreement criticizes claims and evidence, never the people who hold them, and it keeps the conversation open.
reading: Some people in your class, your family or your town may believe the claim you tested. Some may admire Bill Cooper or another writer this course has examined. Respect them. Many came to their views because real institutions really did hide things from them. *Contempt*, treating someone as beneath you, ends a conversation. It never changes a mind.

Respectful disagreement has simple rules. Criticize the claim, not the person. Say what you agree with first. Ask questions instead of scoring points: Where did that come from? What would change your mind? Share a source they can check for themselves. Listen to their answer all the way through. Accept that one talk may not settle anything.

There is one firm line. When a claim targets a whole people, as the Protocols do, you say plainly that it is a forgery and show the proof. You can do that calmly and still respect the person in front of you. The goal of this whole course has been the same from the start. It is not to tell anyone what to believe. It is to help every reader ask *how do we know?* and find the records that answer it.

words.d: treating someone as foolish or beneath you
arguing against a claim while treating the person who holds it with respect
the key question that asks what evidence supports a claim and who can check it

look.title: Two Replies to a Friend
look.text: A friend says: The government hides everything, so Cooper must have been right about aliens. Reply A: That is ridiculous. Only fools believe that. Reply B: You are right that the government hid real programs, like MKUltra. I checked the alien claim too. Here is what the records show. What do you think?
look.prompt: Which reply keeps the conversation going? Rewrite Reply A so it disagrees without contempt.

check.q: What does contempt mean?
choices: Treating someone as foolish or beneath you
check.why: Contempt is treating someone as beneath you, and it ends conversations.

check.q: Which is a rule of respectful disagreement?
choices: Criticize the person, not the claim
Criticize the claim, not the person
check.why: The reading says to criticize the claim, not the person who holds it.

check.q: What does the reading say to do when a claim targets a whole people, as the Protocols do?
choices: Treat it as a matter of opinion
Mock the person who shared it
Say plainly it is a forgery and show the proof, calmly
check.why: The reading draws a firm line: name a forgery as a forgery and show the proof, while still respecting the person.

review.q: Which step comes first when you test a claim?
choices: Narrow the claim and find its earliest source
review.why: The chapter begins with choosing a testable claim and tracing it to its origin.

review.q: What gives a document strong provenance?
choices: A known, clear history of where it came from and who held it
review.why: Provenance is the known history of a document; a long, clear one makes it stronger.

review.q: Why did the Knights of Columbus oath matter as an example?
choices: It was a genuine Catholic oath
It was found in the Copiale Cipher
It was written by George Washington
A House committee condemned it as false, and its purpose was to stir fear of Catholics
review.why: The 1913 House committee condemned the fake oath, which was made to turn voters against Catholics.

review.q: How should a researcher handle the different Maxi Trial conviction counts?
choices: Use whichever number fits the argument
Report a range and name the sources
review.why: The chapter says to report a range, name sources and round when uncertain.

review.q: What made Maya's final paper strong?
choices: She sorted her claim and followed the evidence, even when it changed her view
review.why: Maya sorted her claim into piles and let the evidence set her conclusion.

review.q: Which sentence reports a scholarly debate fairly?
choices: The first Grand Lodge is traditionally dated 1717, though some historians argue 1721
The Grand Lodge was founded in 1721, and anyone who says 1717 is lying
Nobody knows anything about the Grand Lodge
review.why: A fair sentence names both views without calling either side liars.

review.q: What are the four parts of an argument from evidence?
review.why: The chapter names claim, evidence, reasoning and a fairly stated counterclaim.

review.q: What is the goal of respectful disagreement?
choices: To prove the other person is foolish
To avoid talking about hard topics
To keep the conversation open while testing claims with evidence
review.why: Respectful disagreement criticizes claims, not people, and keeps the conversation going.
